scenes.heading: Sooner product, or more at equilibrium?

voiceover.text: A catalyst can make product appear sooner. Does that mean there will be more product when equilibrium is reached? Look at two matching mixtures: the same reacting amounts and starting composition, at the same temperature and volume. Both initially form product. The difference is that only one contains a catalyst. Let us separate the speed of the approach from the mixture they approach.

scenes.heading: Another pathway, lower barriers

voiceover.text: For a reaction to happen, the reacting particles must pass an energy hurdle along a reaction pathway. We call that hurdle activation energy. This diagram plots energy against progress along the pathway, not against time. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower hurdle. At the same temperature, more reacting particles can use that pathway in a given time, so reaction is faster. Measure the forward barrier from the reactant level. Now measure the reverse barrier from the product level. Both barriers are lower on the alternative pathway. The reactant and product energy levels stay where they were.

scenes.heading: A faster approach to the same mixture

voiceover.text: Return to our matching product-forming mixtures. Concentration means amount per volume. The catalysed mixture makes product faster and approaches its equilibrium level sooner. Look at the same earlier time on both curves: it can already contain more product. But the two curves approach the same final concentration. The catalyst changes the pathway and speed, not the equilibrium composition under these matching conditions. These are schematic curves, so they do not give exact experimental times.

scenes.heading: Already at equilibrium?

voiceover.text: What if we add the catalyst to a mixture already at equilibrium? The forward reaction makes product while the reverse reaction uses it. The catalysed system still has equal average opposing rates at equilibrium, so there is no overall change in composition. Faster continuing reactions do not mean product keeps accumulating.

answerSteps: It can contain more B at this earlier time. The catalysed mixture approaches faster.
Both reach the same equilibrium composition. Faster approach does not mean more at equilibrium.

voiceover.text: At an earlier time, the catalysed mixture can contain more B because it is approaching equilibrium faster from this product-forming starting mixture. After both reach equilibrium, their composition is the same under these matching conditions. The catalyst speeds the approach; it does not give a different equilibrium amount.

scenes.heading: Speed, not the equilibrium destination
points: Lower pathway barriers in both directions.
Same equilibrium composition at the same temperature and reacting amounts.

voiceover.text: A useful memory anchor is speed, not the equilibrium destination. Use it with the matching conditions we stated. A lower alternative pathway helps the opposing reactions, and the mixture approaches equilibrium faster. More product during a limited time is different from more product at equilibrium. Next, the equilibrium-expression lesson will give a mathematical way to describe that final mixture. Here are the useful notes.

scenes.heading: Key notes: what to write in your book
points: Catalyst pathway: Lower activation barriers for forward and reverse reactions; endpoint energies stay fixed.
Speed, not destination: Faster approach, same equilibrium composition under matching conditions.
Earlier versus final: More product can be present earlier from a product-forming mixture.
